labels.reason: Historical reviewer: The rule fires on nearly every structure that is not a canonical subject-verb-object sentence: (1) transcript/dialogue turns ("Marc: Seven.", "Marc: Menus.", multiple podcast exchange lines) which are inherently short; (2) poem, toast, and event-recap verse fragments embedded in blog posts; (3) image captions ("Left: black and white. Middle: automatically colorized."); (4) navigation labels and section headings ("Forming the Company", "Latest Content by Marc"); (5) rhetorical questions used as valid literary devices ("Who better to help U.S. entrepreneurs"); (6) terse imperative advice ("Full stop."); (7) line-wrapped plain-text from Paul Graham essays where the wrapper cuts mid-sentence. The rule has no content-type or structural-context awareness and conflates intentional stylistic brevity with AI slop fragment lists.

original.excerpt: [business/a16z] (Fragment stack found: Left: black and white. Middl) Left: black and white. Middle: automatically colorized. Right: true color. (Source)
